02

One release-week scenario, run through three strategies

"Your team is dropping V2.0 of your Ignition project next week. Mid-week, an end user reports a P1 bug in v1.2 that's already running in production. You need to ship the v1.2 hotfix today AND keep V2.0 on track."the scenario, docs/branching-strategies.md

  1. in productionv1.2 is livethe code customers run
  2. in flightV2.0 work is opennot merged, not finished
  3. mid-weekP1 bug in v1.2hotfix must ship today
  4. next weekV2.0 shipswith the fix inside it
1 OF 3

Git Flow: main and develop, plus feature, release and hotfix branches

2 OF 3

GitHub Flow: one main, short-lived branches that return through a PR

3 OF 3

Trunk-based: everyone on main, branches live hours, flags hide unfinished work

03

Pick the strategy that fits your team's reality

Your situationBest fit
Single SaaS product, continuous deploy, 2 to 10 engineersGitHub Flow
Multiple released versions live at once, and you still patch the old ones (a v1.2 hotfix while v2.0 ships)Git Flow: release and hotfix branches give each version a place to live
Strict regulatory environment, lengthy validation per releaseGit Flow: release branches make audit easy
Feature flags and fast, trusted CI already in place, and you want to integrate continuously to mainTrunk-based: needs both; it's GitHub Flow with the branch life cut to hours
Brand-new team, learning Git for the first timeGitHub Flow: lowest cognitive overhead
The real question is just oneIs more than one version live at a time? No: GitHub Flow (trunk-based is its high-discipline extreme). Yes: Git Flow. The labs use GitHub Flow; the stretch lets you feel Git Flow's double-merge. For your team, pick what fits, not what sounds most sophisticated.

04

The life of a feature branch, from branch to merge

05

A bad PR and a good PR, side by side

The bad PR

  • Title: "update stuff"
  • 800-line diff across 12 files
  • No description
  • Mixes a rename, a bugfix and a feature
  • Leaves validate.sh red

The good PR

  • Title: fix(display): handle null readings without crashing
  • 6-line diff in one file
  • Clear What / Why / How to test
  • One concern only
  • validate.sh green
The rule of thumbIf you catch yourself writing "and" in the PR title, split the PR.
06

Four properties that make a PR easy to review

1

Small

  • Under 200 lines of diff, ideally under 50
  • Reviewers find more bugs in small PRs because they actually read them
  • A 1,000-line PR gets rubber-stamped, however rigorous the reviewer feels
2

One concern

  • A bugfix is not a refactor
  • A rename is not a feature
  • A formatting pass is not a code change
3

Self-describing

  • What does this change? One sentence
  • Why now? The bug, ticket or request
  • How does a reviewer verify it? Commands to run
4

Tested

  • A test that would have caught the bug, or an explicit manual test plan in "How to test"
  • In this lab: scripts/validate.sh plus running the function you changed (python3 -c)
In order of importanceThe PR template enforces 2 to 4 by structure; smallness is on you. The fuller toolkit (optional): docs/pr-review-style.md.
07

Label each review comment so the author knows how to react

LabelMeaningExample
praise:Something genuinely good: tells the author what's workingpraise: nicely focused diff, easy to review.
suggestion:A specific, optional improvement: accept, decline with reasoning, or discusssuggestion: collapse these two ifs into one.
issue:Something that should change before mergeissue: this still throws on a null reading; format_reading(None, '°C') errors instead of showing a placeholder.
nitpick: question: thought: chore:The fuller set, when you want it: docs/pr-review-style.md and conventionalcomments.org
ToneLabels don't make rude feedback polite. If you wouldn't say it in person, don't write it in the PR. Async amplifies tone: neutral in your head reads cold on screen. "?" is not a review comment.
08

Three review verdicts, and how the author responds

The reviewer ends with a verdict

ApproveHappy to merge as-is; trivial nitpicks are fine inside an approve

Request changesThere's at least one issue: the author must address

Comment-onlyYou read it but aren't voting: not your area, or someone already approved

Common mistakeRequest-changes for nitpicks: friction without value.
The author negotiates: authors have rights too
  • Respond to every comment: a +1, a reply, or a fix-up commit. Silence reads as ignoring the reviewer.
  • Declining is allowed: turning down a suggestion with reasoning is a valid response.
  • Don't force-push during review: it nukes the reviewer's context. Additive commits now, squash on merge if you must.
09

Three ways to merge an approved PR on GitHub

Merge commit

--no-ff: keeps every commit and preserves the branch shape in the graph.

This course: Create a merge commit

Squash and merge

The whole PR becomes one commit on main.

Rebase and merge

Replays the commits linearly onto main, no merge commit.

Not a preferencePick the method your team agreed on, deliberately, not whatever the dropdown remembers. Verdicts and merge methods are both choices your team agreement should make for you.
10

Open, review and merge a PR on your fork

  1. Open the PR. After a push, your fork's page shows Compare & pull request. Set base repository to <you>/cicd-for-ignition (it defaults to the course repo), base main, compare your branch. Fill in What / Why / How to test.
  2. Invite a reviewer. On your fork: Settings → Collaborators → Add people. Once they accept, pick them under Reviewers in the PR's sidebar.
  3. Review. Files changed tab, + next to a line to comment (Start a review), then Review changes: Comment, Approve or Request changes, and Submit review.
  4. Merge. Merge pull request (dropdown: Create a merge commit), Confirm merge, then Delete branch.
Two reposYour fork is origin, the course repo you forked is upstream. In this course every PR goes into your own fork.
# first push of a new branch: -u links it to your fork
git push -u origin feature/v2-silo-detail
git push                        # every later push

# tags never ride along: push each one by name
git push origin lab02-v1.2.0

# gh repo fork --clone made the COURSE repo gh's default
gh repo set-default --view      # must print YOUR fork
gh repo set-default <you>/cicd-for-ignition
gh pr create                    # PR into your fork's main

# reviewer: run the PR's code locally, then go back
gh pr checkout <n> --repo <author>/cicd-for-ignition --detach
git switch -
11

Commit messages in the Conventional Commits format

feattype: what kind(viewsscope: where): add v2.0 silo detail viewsummary: what, imperative
Two conventions, two jobsConventional Commits label commit messages (feat:, fix:); Conventional Comments label review comments (praise:, suggestion:, issue:). People scan history faster, and release tools can read it too.
  1. fixpatch: v1.2.1
  2. featminor: v1.3.0
  3. feat!:breaking, major: v2.0.0

Once releases are automated, the type picks the version bump. Today you need feat and fix.

TypeUse it forExample
featA new feature or capabilityfeat(views): add v2.0 silo detail view
fixA bug fixfix(display): placeholder for null readings
docsDocumentation onlydocs(readme): explain GATEWAY_PORT
refactorRestructure without changing behaviourrefactor(display): reuse lab.util.to_float
testAdd or fix teststest(display): cover None readings
chore ciTooling, dependencies, pipelinesci: run validate.sh on every PR

An Ignition project in Git

  1. Filesthe project on disk
  2. Ignore ruleswhat belongs in the repo
  3. Diffsa save becomes a diff
  4. Scansediting outside the Designer
12

An Ignition 8.3 project is a folder of small text files

projects/lab-project/ in this lab's repo
projects/lab-project/
├── project.json                 # manifest: title, enabled, parent
├── com.inductiveautomation.perspective/  # one folder per module
│   ├── views/pages/overview/    # one folder per resource
│   │   ├── view.json            # the payload: the whole view
│   │   ├── thumbnail.png        # Designer preview (binary)
│   │   └── resource.json        # manifest: scope, files list
│   ├── page-config/  config.json + resource.json
│   └── session-props/  props.json + resource.json
└── ignition/script-python/lab/
    ├── display/  code.py + resource.json  # lab.display
    └── util/     code.py + resource.json  # lab.util
  • Resources are folders: a resource.json manifest plus the payload: view.json for a view, code.py for a script library.
  • Namespaced by module: com.inductiveautomation.perspective and ignition/script-python each own a subtree.
  • All JSON and Python: diffable, blame-able, branchable, reviewable. The exception: thumbnail.png, a binary Git tracks but can't diff.
  • Bind-mounted: the compose stack mounts only ./projects into the gateway, so it serves whatever branch you have checked out. Gateway config stays in a named volume (Lab 04's story).
13

What to commit and what to put in .gitignore

If a human authored it, commit it. If the gateway (re)generates it, ignore it.

Commit: human-authored

  • project.json: the project manifest
  • resource.json + payloads: view.json, code.py, config.json
  • .gitignore, .gitattributes, PR template: the repo's own rules
  • docker-compose.yml, scripts/, docs

Ignore: generated or secret

  • **/.resources/: the gateway's blob store, regenerated on boot or scan
  • **/*.digest.json, migration-log-*.md: gateway churn
  • .env: credentials never enter history (commit .env.example)
  • OS and editor junk: .DS_Store, .idea/, __pycache__/
The line-ending trapThis lab's .gitattributes forces LF. Without it, Windows clones put CRLF in Ignition's JSON: noisy diffs on files you never touched, and confused project scans. Gateway-generated files in git status? Fix your ignore rules before committing.
14

A Designer save is a file write, so it's a diff

  1. Designer savethe gateway writes JSON
  2. Project fileson disk, bind-mounted
  3. git statusexactly what changed
  4. git add -pa scoped commit
  5. A small PRa one-line diff, read in ten seconds
  • In this lab your editor plays the Designer: same files, same diffs.
  • A bind mount links the container's project folder to a folder on your machine: one shared folder, not a copy. A Designer save lands in your files; a file edit reaches the Designer. No exporting, no syncing.
  • Read your own diff before you commit: the cheapest review you'll ever get, and the habit that keeps Ignition PRs small.
# git diff after changing one label text
--- a/…/views/pages/overview/view.json
+++ b/…/views/pages/overview/view.json
         "letterSpacing": "1.5px"
       },
-      "text": "KILN TEMP"
+      "text": "KILN TEMPERATURE"
     },

# a script change: plain Python diffs
--- a/…/script-python/lab/display/code.py
+++ b/…/script-python/lab/display/code.py
 def format_reading(value, units):
+    if value is None:
+        return "%s %s" % (PLACEHOLDER, units)
     return "%.1f %s" % (value, units)
15

Edit in VS Code, then scan so the gateway picks it up

The catchEdits made through VS Code are not picked up automatically by the running gateway. Trigger a project scan and a config scan through the gateway's API.
Project scanreloads views and scripts
Config scanreloads gateway config files
Recommended VS Code extensions
  • Flint for Ignition: Ignition project support in the editor
  • Docker: manage the lab's containers from VS Code
  • Remote Development pack: edit inside the container or over SSH as if local
# edit a file in VS Code…
$ code projects/lab-project/.../code.py

# …then tell the gateway to pick it up:
$ scripts/scan.sh
POST /data/api/v1/scan/projects   # project resources
POST /data/api/v1/scan/config     # gateway config files
   header: X-Ignition-API-Token: <name>:<secret>
gateway now serves your edit
16

Set up the scan API key, or let Flint scan for you

1 · No "scan permission"

The key gets a custom security level, and that level must be in Gateway Write Permissions.

2 · The full token

The header value is the full name:secret the UI shows. The secret alone is a 401.

3 · HTTPS-only by default

On this lab's plain-http gateway, disable "Require secure connections for API Keys".

Step-by-step in .env.example.

Flint scans for youThe lab's gateway installs the Project Scan Endpoint module at boot (from third-party-modules/). Flint calls the scan API plus its endpoint, POST /data/project-scan-endpoint/scan, which also makes an open Designer reload. Same API key, in .flint/tokens/local-api.json. Source: github.com/bw-design-group/ignition-project-scan-endpoint
17

Run a script function on your laptop before you open the PR

Prove it worksvalidate.sh only proves a file parses. To show a fix works, call the function with the inputs that matter, and paste the command plus its output into How to test.
  • The gateway won't show it: the overview's kiln tile always passes 162.0, so the None case never reaches the screen.
  • runpy.run_path loads code.py like a module and hands you its functions. Call them with a normal value, zero and None.
  • Python 3 is not Jython 2.7, but small pure functions like format_reading behave the same in both.
  • The limit: code that calls another project library (lab.util.to_float) only runs on the gateway, where lab exists. Locally it raises NameError.
# from the lab folder
python3 -c "import runpy
p = 'projects/lab-project/ignition/script-python/lab/display/code.py'
f = runpy.run_path(p)['format_reading']
for v in (162.0, 0, None): print(f(v, '°C'))"

# before the fix
162.0 °C
0.0 °C
TypeError: must be real number, not NoneType

# after the fix
162.0 °C
0.0 °C
-- °C
